agent.definition: A system in which a model decides, in a loop, which actions (tool calls) to take toward a goal, and when it is done.

tool.definition: A function, API or service an agent can call to read data or take an action. The model asks for the call; the runtime (or, for built-in tools, the provider's service) runs it.

workflow.definition: Control flow the designer defines in advance (sequences, branches, loops), possibly with model calls inside steps. A model may pick a predefined branch, but it never invents the path.

determinism spectrum.definition: The range of designs ordered by how much the system decides for itself: a chatbot acts only when the user asks, a workflow follows the designer's path, and an agent directs its own steps. More autonomy buys flexibility and costs predictability.

gemini enterprise.definition: Google's platform where employees discover, create, run and govern AI agents, including the low-code Workflow Builder.

agent platform.definition: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: Google Cloud's platform to build, scale, govern and optimise agents, announced in April 2026 as the evolution of Vertex AI.

agent runtime.definition: Agent Platform's managed runtime that deploys, operates and scales agents, used with its Sessions and Memory Bank services (formerly Agent Engine).

hybrid agent.definition: A system that combines low-code agents (for example a Workflow Builder workflow) with code-built agents or tools (for example an ADK agent or an MCP server) that the low-code side calls.

trajectory.definition: The sequence of tool calls (and other intermediate steps) an agent took before it answered. Evaluating it checks the path, not just the final response.

offline evaluation.definition: Running an agent on a fixed dataset of cases before release, so that versions can be compared and regressions caught before users see them.

online monitoring.definition: Measuring a deployed agent's quality on live traffic, through traces, logs and metrics, to catch what the offline dataset missed and what changes after launch.

golden dataset.definition: A curated, fixed set of inputs with the outputs you would accept (for an agent, the expected tool calls as well as the expected reply), run on every version so results can be compared.

evalset.definition: An ADK file of eval cases, each a session with its own id and initial state, often multi-turn, used for integration-style evaluation of an agent.

user simulation.definition: An evaluation method in which a model plays the user, generating each user turn from a starting prompt, a conversation plan and optionally a persona, so branching conversations can be tested.

function calling.definition: A model capability: given function declarations, the model can return a structured request to call one of them with arguments, instead of text. The application or runtime executes the call and sends the result back.

function declaration.definition: The name, description and parameter schema that tell a model a tool exists and when to use it. In ADK it is generated from a function's name, docstring and type hints.

react.definition: Reason and act: a pattern in which a model alternates reasoning steps with actions such as tool calls, each result informing the next step (Yao et al., 2022).

max iterations.definition: A cap on how many times an agent loop may run, so a loop that is not converging stops. ADK counts it in model calls per run (max_llm_calls); a LoopAgent's max_iterations is a separate cap on cycles of a workflow loop.

adk.definition: Agent Development Kit: Google's open-source framework for building agents in code (Python, TypeScript, Go, Java and Kotlin).

llmagent.definition: ADK's model-driven agent (alias Agent), configured with a name, model, instruction, tools, optional sub-agents and callbacks.

agenttool.definition: An ADK wrapper that lets one agent call another like a function tool. The wrapped agent's answer returns to the caller, which keeps control.

callback.definition: A function ADK runs at a fixed point in the loop: before or after an agent, a model call or a tool call. It can let the step proceed, skip it with its own result, or replace the output.

min instances.definition: The number of instances a service keeps running even with no traffic, so requests avoid cold starts; you pay for them while they wait.

container concurrency.definition: The number of requests one instance of a service handles at the same time.

session.definition: The record of one conversation between a user and an agent: its messages, the agent's events and its working state. A session service is where an agent stores sessions.

slm.definition: Small language model: fewer parameters than a large model, so lower cost and latency per request, but a narrower range of tasks it handles well.

maas.definition: Model as a service: a model called through a managed API endpoint, pay-as-you-go by default (reserved capacity is an option), with no serving infrastructure to run.

model garden.definition: Google Cloud's catalogue of Google, partner and open models, with the serving options each one offers (managed endpoints or self-deployment).

self-deployed model.definition: A model whose weights you deploy to an endpoint or cluster you control (for example Gemma on an Agent Platform endpoint or GKE), paying for that compute while it runs.

flow.definition: In Dialogflow CX and CX Agent Studio, a group of pages that models one conversation topic as a state machine.

page.definition: A state in a Dialogflow CX flow, with its own routes, parameters and event handlers; exactly one page is current at a time.

transition route.definition: A Dialogflow CX rule with an intent requirement, a condition requirement or both, which can reply and move the conversation to another page.

event handler.definition: A Dialogflow CX rule that responds to an event, such as no-match or no-input, usually by replying or reprompting.

few-shot example.definition: A sample exchange included in an agent's instructions to show the model the behaviour or format you want.

workflow builder.definition: The low-code tool in Gemini Enterprise for building chat agents and workflows without code (formerly Agent Designer).

trigger.definition: What starts a Workflow Builder workflow: manual (an @-mention in chat), a schedule, or an event in a connected app.

gemini agent step.definition: A Workflow Builder workflow step in which a model acts on instructions, knowledge and connectors, and returns text or JSON for later steps.

prompt injection.definition: Input crafted to override an LLM application's instructions. In a direct injection the person using the application writes it; in an indirect one it arrives in content the application reads.

indirect prompt injection.definition: A prompt injection carried by content an agent reads rather than by the person using it: a web page, a document, an email or a tool's output. It can be invisible to humans.

excessive agency.definition: An agent holding more than its task needs: more tools, broader permissions or more freedom to act without a check. It decides how much damage a manipulation or a model mistake can do.

agent identity.definition: A dedicated identity for each agent on Google Cloud, based on SPIFFE, with its own certificate-bound credentials. You grant roles to it directly, and audit logs name the agent.

spiffe.definition: An open standard for identifying software workloads with cryptographic identities, such as X.509 certificates, rather than shared secrets.

principal access boundary.definition: An IAM policy that defines which resources a principal is eligible to access. It can block access regardless of the principal's role grants (for the permissions it supports), but it never grants access.

agent gateway.definition: Google Cloud's managed gateway for agent traffic, including calls to MCP servers. It enforces access policies on that traffic, can screen it with Model Armor, and records it so it can be monitored.

agent registry.definition: Google Cloud's catalogue of registered agents, MCP servers, endpoints and skills. It gives each one identifiers for discovery and for the policies and route rules that govern it.

oauth 2.0.definition: An authorisation framework that lets an application obtain limited access to an HTTP service with access tokens, either on behalf of a user who approves it or on its own behalf.

openid connect.definition: An identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0. It adds an ID token with claims about how the user signed in, so an application can know who the user is.

authconfig.definition: In ADK, the object that pairs a tool's AuthScheme (how the API expects credentials) with its AuthCredential (the initial information to start the flow).

model armor.definition: Google Cloud's service that screens prompts and responses, for example for prompt injection and jailbreaks, harmful content, malicious URLs and sensitive data, using templates of filters and confidence thresholds.

floor setting.definition: A minimum set of Model Armor requirements at organisation, folder or project level. No template can be created or updated to be less strict than the floor.

sensitive data protection.definition: Google Cloud's service for finding and de-identifying sensitive data. Inside Model Armor, basic mode inspects a fixed set of infoTypes, and advanced mode uses its templates and can de-identify.

human in the loop.definition: A design where a person must approve an agent's action, such as an irreversible tool call, before it runs.

span.definition: One timed operation in a trace, such as a model call or a tool call, nested under the span of the operation that started it. Its length shows where the time went.

reasoning loop.definition: An agent failure in which the model repeats the same tool call or step, often with the same arguments, without making progress, until a cap or timeout stops it.

drift.definition: A deployed agent's quality degrading over time as the model, prompts, tools, data or users change, while the service stays up and fast.

tool trajectory match.definition: Comparing an agent's actual tool calls (name and arguments) with the expected ones, in one of three modes: exact, in-order (extra calls allowed) or any-order (extra calls and any order allowed).

gen ai evaluation service.definition: Agent Platform's managed evaluation for models and agents, with rubric-based (including adaptive), computation-based and custom function metrics scored where needed by a judge model.

context window.definition: The tokens a model sees in one call: instructions, tool declarations, history, recalled memory, retrieved content and the new message. Its size is a limit, and every token in it costs time and money.

context caching.definition: Reusing the processing of a prompt prefix that repeats across calls, which cuts the cost and latency of that prefix. The cached tokens still count in the context window.

history compaction.definition: Summarising or trimming a conversation's earlier turns so each call carries less history, while keeping the most recent turns as they were.

sequential agent.definition: An orchestration pattern (and ADK's SequentialAgent class, deprecated in Python 2.x in favour of Workflow) that runs sub-agents in a fixed order, each able to use the previous one's result.

parallel agent.definition: An orchestration pattern (and ADK's ParallelAgent class, deprecated in Python 2.x in favour of Workflow) that runs independent sub-agents at the same time and gathers their results; the branches share session state.

loop agent.definition: An orchestration pattern (and ADK's LoopAgent class, deprecated in Python 2.x in favour of Workflow) that repeats sub-agents until an exit condition is met or an iteration cap is reached.

graph workflow.definition: Orchestration defined as nodes and edges, with routed branches, fan-out and join, and back-edges for loops; ADK 2.0's Workflow class.

mcp.definition: Model Context Protocol: an open standard for offering tools to agents. An MCP server publishes tools with names, descriptions and parameter schemas; an MCP client, such as an agent, lists and calls them.

a2a.definition: Agent2Agent: an open protocol for independent agents to discover each other through agent cards and work together on tasks, without seeing each other's internals.

agent card.definition: A JSON document an A2A agent publishes, usually at /.well-known/agent-card.json, advertising its skills, endpoint, capabilities and required authentication.

remote agent.definition: An agent running in another process or service, often owned by another team, that a client agent reaches over A2A.

google cloud mcp servers.definition: Remote MCP servers that run on Google's infrastructure and offer an HTTP endpoint for a Google Cloud service, such as BigQuery or GKE, with access controlled through IAM.

mcp toolbox for databases.definition: An open-source MCP server that exposes database queries as agent tools, each defined in configuration with a fixed statement and typed parameters.

rag.definition: Retrieval-augmented generation: before the model answers, the system retrieves relevant passages from your documents and puts them in the model's context.

embedding.definition: A vector of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text, so texts with similar meaning sit close together and can be found by similarity search.

top-k.definition: How many of the highest-ranked retrieved chunks are passed on to the model (or to the next retrieval step).

reranking.definition: Rescoring a wider set of retrieved candidates with a stronger relevance model, so only the most relevant few reach the model.

rag engine.definition: Agent Platform's managed RAG pipeline and corpus service: it ingests, chunks, embeds, indexes and retrieves your documents, with configurable chunking, embedding model, vector database and reranking.

session state.definition: Key-value data an agent and its code read and write during a session. In ADK a key's prefix sets its scope: none (this session), user:, app: or temp:.

memory bank.definition: Agent Platform's managed long-term memory: it extracts facts from conversations with an LLM, consolidates them with what it already holds, keeps them isolated per scope (such as agent and user), and returns the relevant ones in later sessions.

mcp server.definition: A program that offers tools (and optionally resources and prompts) to an agent over the Model Context Protocol. The agent is the client that lists and calls them.

skill.definition: A folder of instructions and supporting files, headed by a SKILL.md with a name and description, that a coding agent loads on demand for a kind of task.

progressive disclosure.definition: Loading a skill in steps: its name and description are always in context, its full instructions load when a task matches, and its other files load only when needed.

antigravity.definition: Google's agentic development environment, offered as a desktop app, a CLI (agy), IDE extensions and a Python SDK.

rule.definition: Persistent guidance for a coding agent in a Markdown file, in its context always or when a trigger such as a file pattern matches. The model reads it and decides; nothing enforces it.

hook.definition: A command the coding agent's harness runs on a lifecycle event, such as before or after a tool call, whatever the model decides. A hook that runs before a tool call can block it.

subagent.definition: A delegated agent with its own instructions, context and optionally its own model and tool list, which takes a task from the main agent and returns a result.

plugin.definition: A versioned package that bundles a coding agent's customisations, such as skills, hooks, subagents and MCP servers (and, in Antigravity, rules), so a team can install and update them together.

skill registry.definition: An Agent Platform repository, in Preview, that stores versioned agent skills in a Google Cloud project for agents to search and load. Google plans to make it part of Agent Registry.

agents cli.definition: Google's command-line tool and set of skills that teach a coding agent the agent lifecycle on Google Cloud: scaffold, evaluate, deploy, publish and observe. It is a tool for coding agents, not a coding agent itself.

generator-critic.definition: An agent design pattern (also called reflection) in which one agent drafts and a critic checks the draft against criteria, approving it or returning fixes, in a loop that needs an exit and a cap.

plan-then-execute.definition: An agent design pattern in which a planner writes the whole plan first, a gate (a person or a policy check) approves it, and only then do executors carry out the steps.
